title: We’re In A Relationship Recession. Is Single The New Power Move?
summary: An op-ed style episode arguing that we are in a romantic 'relationship recession' with more single people than ever, set against a mini-history of the four waves of feminism and a case study of Bumble's Whitney Wolfe Herd. Jean maps the economics of a recession (monetary easing, fiscal policy, structural reform) onto dating, Cherie offers a 'pattern interruption' framework, and the takeaways are to decenter men, get your own bag, build platonic community and celebrate non-traditional wins.

ideas.idea: We are in a relationship recession: for the first time in history there are more single people than ever, and the number of singles globally has grown by over 100 million in ten years.
ideas.detail: The Economist reports that among Americans 25-34 the share living without a spouse or partner has doubled over five decades to 50 percent of men and 41 percent of women. Stanford sociologist Michael Rosenfeld attributes 13.7 million extra US singles in 2022 to the pandemic's reduction in dating.

ideas.idea: Underneath the shifting archetypes (housewife, hippie, girl boss, trad wife) there is one constant expectation of women: to be the nurturing mother, which is why 'having it all' is only ever applied to women.
ideas.detail: A successful man just has to be successful; a woman must be successful, birth and raise children, and be a fabulous mother. Cherie is angry at the unfairness but grateful that financial freedom now lets women choose rather than stay stuck.

ideas.idea: Women's legal personhood and right to choose their own archetype is less than 100 years old, spanning four waves of feminism.
ideas.detail: First wave (1920s-40s) brought voting, education and property rights; second wave (60s-80s, Betty Friedan's The Feminine Mystique) fought workplace discrimination and the assumption women are most satisfied at home; third wave (1990s-2010s) added intersectionality. Columbia University only admitted women in the 1970s, which is why Barnard exists.

ideas.idea: Whitney Wolfe Herd is the original girl boss, but the media celebrated her partly because she still fulfilled the archetype of beautiful, brilliant mother, setting a possibly unattainable bar.
ideas.detail: She rang the NASDAQ bell with her 18-month-old son on her hip as the world's youngest female billionaire and youngest woman to take a company public. Cherie saw her speak twice at Stanford GSB and, as a new grad at LinkedIn, recalls women thinking 'this is what it could be' while also wondering 'you good?' and whether she 'girl bossed too close to the sun'.

ideas.idea: The trad wife resurgence is a pendulum swing: women who ground themselves down in corporate girl-boss jobs in the 2010s burned out and now crave softness and the feminine.
ideas.detail: The hosts recall day-to-night outfits and change-of-shoes bags of the 9-to-5 grind, and point to Ballerina Farm's Hannah Neeleman and Nara Smith as the new archetype of wanting to make sourdough at home.

ideas.idea: The next wave of feminism is the ability to choose, girl boss or trad wife, and that choice is only real when you have your own financial freedom.
ideas.detail: 'Get your own bag and make your own decisions' so every choice is made with a clear head and no external force pushing you into one archetype. The hosts note choices are now also projected publicly on social media and shaped by whether your friend group shares your archetype.

ideas.idea: The 'embarrassing to have a boyfriend' discourse is partly structural: over 50 percent of women now hold higher-education degrees versus 39 percent of men, so women who want to date at their level face a shortage.
ideas.detail: A Vogue article from October declared having a boyfriend embarrassing and dominated discourse for three months. Cherie says she wants a partner who is the same or better than her in education and hobbies, someone she can respect and learn from, and the pool often does not meet the mark.

ideas.idea: Most single people still want a relationship: across 14 countries only 40 percent say they are not interested, and 27 percent cite being too busy, too old, or unwanted.
ideas.detail: Cited from an Economist study from the prior November, reframed by the hosts as a global and generational issue, with the 100 million new singles as a large pool of potential first dates.

ideas.idea: A relationship recession works like an economic one: demand collapses, confidence drops and people stop investing in their futures, with rising costs (emotional labor, therapy-speak, dating burnout) and capital hoarding (guarding hearts, bodies and time).
ideas.detail: Jean, an econ major, frames it: in a financial recession borrowing is too risky, in a relationship recession emotional vulnerability is too risky. Situationships are 'microdosing vulnerability'. Choosing a candle, PJs and a movie over a possibly-nothing date is capital hoarding.

ideas.idea: Fix the recession with 'monetary easing': normalize low-stakes honesty so you communicate feelings in small doses instead of building up to one giant scary conversation, which beats ghosting.
ideas.detail: Examples: 'I really like you but I'm scared' or 'where do you think this is going?' Small honest doses invite the other person to respond in kind; ghosting only adds to the problem.

ideas.idea: 'Fiscal policy' for dating means using your own power to build community, like organizing group dinners where each friend brings someone new.
ideas.detail: Creating environments to meet more people, without the pressure of explicit coupling up, stimulates demand the way government spending does.

ideas.idea: 'Structural reform' means decentering men: celebrate Galentine's Day alongside Valentine's Day and treat platonic love as equally worthy of celebration.
ideas.detail: Galentine's Day was coined by Amy Poehler's Leslie Knope on Parks and Recreation. Loving relationships come in many forms and need not be romantic or partnered.

ideas.idea: Use 'pattern interruption', borrowed from tech behavioral design, to break your dating routine: swipe on people outside your type and drop superficial filters like six-feet-and-above.
ideas.detail: Dating apps are built for shallowness. Cherie points to Charlotte and Harry in Sex and the City as a couple she would never have considered who became the happiest love of Charlotte's life.

ideas.idea: Ask friends to set you up and go in blind, without researching the person, because social accountability improves matches and pre-research kills chemistry.
ideas.detail: Jean is currently testing this: a friend connected her with someone, and she deliberately did not follow him back on Instagram to avoid preconceived notions, though she admits checking his LinkedIn 'for the facts'.

ideas.idea: Multiple things can be true at once: you can want a partnered relationship and still be fully empowered, single and powerful, or in an unconventional relationship, as long as you have autonomy.
ideas.detail: The hosts note they are the first women in their bloodline to be single at this age and living alone, in a moment when that can still feel empowered. The romantic recession is counterbalanced by a resurgence of platonic relationships and community.

ideas.idea: Celebrate non-traditional wins with your girlfriends, like passing the bar, a promotion or buying a house, since society only builds in celebrations for engagements, weddings and babies.
ideas.detail: Cherie wants to try a TikTok 'celebration cake' with little flags for each win. Jean's friend bought a house in the Palisades on her own and the group celebrated it together.
